title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #16**: Odd Integers Not of the Form 2^k + p

**Question**: Is the set of odd integers NOT representable as 2^k + p the union of an arithmetic progression and a density-0 set?

**Status**: SOLVED (DISPROVED - Chen 2023)

**Answer**: NO. The exceptional set has more complex structure.

Erdős called this conjecture 'rather silly' - and he was right to be skeptical!
mathContext: OEIS A006285 lists the exceptional odd integers: 1, 127, 149, 251, 331, 337, 373, 509, 599, 701, ...

title: Background: Romanoff's Theorem
content:
**Romanoff (1934)**: A positive proportion of odd integers CAN be written as 2^k + p.

The 'exceptional' odd integers are those that CANNOT.

**Examples** (OEIS A006285):
1, 127, 149, 251, 331, 337, 373, 509, 599, 701, ...

Note: 1 is trivially exceptional (no prime + power of 2 equals 1).
mathContext: Romanoff's proof uses a probabilistic heuristic made rigorous: for a random odd $n$, the 'probability' that $n - 2^k$ is prime is $\sim 1/\log(n - 2^k)$, and summing over $k = 1, \ldots, \lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ gives expected count $\sim \log_2 n / \log n \to \infty$. A sieve argument converts this into a positive density result. The exceptional set $E$ (OEIS A006285) has density $\approx 0.09$ among all positive integers.

title: Romanoff Numbers and Exceptional Set
mathContext: The condition k ≥ 1 ensures 2^k ≥ 2. For n to be Romanoff, we need n - 2^k prime for some valid k.

title: Exceptional Characterization
content:
Documented (not formalized) as a source comment: n ∈ ExceptionalSet ⟺ ∀ k ≥ 1, 2^k < n → n − 2^k is NOT prime. (The formalized `mem_exceptionalSet_iff`, in the Foundational Lemmas section below, unfolds membership to `Odd n ∧ ¬ IsRomanoff n` directly — this alternative composite-subtraction characterization is not itself a separate Lean declaration.)

**Interpretation**: An odd n is exceptional iff EVERY valid subtraction leaves a composite.
mathContext: This gives a computational test: check n - 2, n - 4, n - 8, ... until 2^k ≥ n. If all are composite, n is exceptional.

title: Density and Romanoff's Theorem
content: **density A N** = |A ∩ [0,N]| / (N+1) and **lowerDensity A** = liminf of density as N → ∞ are real `noncomputable def`s. Romanoff's 1934 theorem (positive density of odd integers are Romanoff) is documented in a source comment only — no Lean declaration formalizes it here; the file's machine-checked density result instead concerns the *exceptional* set (see Density Bounds / full-strength sections below).
mathContext: The lower density uses infimum over all sufficiently large N. This is stronger than just 'infinitely many'.

title: Covering Congruences
content:
**IsCoveringSystem residues** (a real `def`): the residue classes cover all integers, ∀ n : ℤ, ∃ (r, m) ∈ residues, n ≡ r (mod m).

Erdős's 1950 claim that the exceptional set contains an infinite arithmetic progression is stated here as a source comment only — but it is not left unformalized: `exceptionalSet_infinite` (in the infinite-progression section below) proves exactly this via the explicit covering progression 7629217 + q·11184810, axiom-free.
mathContext: Erdős's covering system uses moduli $\{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24\}$ with $\text{lcm} = 24$ and $\sum 1/m_i = 1$. For each modulus $m_i$, the residue class is chosen so that $2^k \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}$ for the corresponding $k$-values, forcing composites at every step — this file's later sections carry out the construction fully, in place of the axiom this comment might once have suggested.

title: The Conjecture (FALSE)
content:
**ErdosConjecture16** (a real `def`, formalized): ExceptionalSet = (arithmetic progression) ∪ (density-0 set), i.e. ∃ a d > 0 with lowerDensity(ExceptionalSet \ {a + md}) = 0.

Chen's 2023 disproof (¬ErdosConjecture16) is documented in a source comment only — no `chen_disproof` declaration exists in the Lean source; the analytic argument is beyond current Mathlib.
mathContext: Erdős hoped the exceptional set had simple structure, self-deprecatingly calling the conjecture 'rather silly.' Chen showed it contains multiple 'essentially different' parts with positive density, but this disproof itself is not machine-checked here.

title: Complex Structure
content: Documented (not formalized) consequences of Chen's disproof: the exceptional set likely contains multiple 'independent' arithmetic progressions, may exhibit fractal-like or quasi-random structure, and connects to deep questions about prime distribution. No single progression captures the whole exceptional set — none of this is stated as a Lean declaration.
mathContext: This is a consequence of Chen's disproof. The exceptional set has rich, possibly fractal-like structure, beyond what the single covering-congruence progression formalized elsewhere in this file produces.

title: Known Exceptional Numbers
content:
**OEIS A006285**: 1, 127, 149, 251, 331, 337, 373, 509, 599, 701, 757, 809, 877, ...

Stated here as a source comment (not itself a Lean declaration), but 127, 149, 251, and 331 are each machine-checked exceptional in the Foundational Lemmas section below, via the `Decidable (IsRomanoff n)` instance and `decide` — e.g. for 127: 127 − 2 = 125 = 5³, 127 − 4 = 123 = 3×41, 127 − 8 = 119 = 7×17, 127 − 16 = 111 = 3×37, 127 − 32 = 95 = 5×19, 127 − 64 = 63 = 7×9 are all composite, and 2^7 = 128 > 127 closes the case.
mathContext: 127 is the smallest non-trivial exceptional number. The listed verification shows all valid subtractions yield composites — genuinely machine-checked below via `decide`, not merely asserted.

title: Erdős's Covering System
content: **erdosCovering** = [(0,2), (0,3), (1,4), (1,6), (3,8), (7,12), (23,24)], a real `def` (a `List (ℕ × ℕ)` of residue/modulus pairs). Its covering property (`erdosCovering_isCoveringSystem`) is proved axiom-free by `decide` in the Foundational Lemmas section below. The consequence that for exceptional n each n − 2^k is divisible by a small prime is not stated as one theorem about `erdosCovering` directly — it is instead proved constructively, prime-by-prime, via the covering-congruence obstruction mechanism (`covering_prime_not_prime_sub` and its concrete instances) later in the file.
mathContext: The covering $\{(0,2), (0,3), (1,4), (1,6), (3,8), (7,12), (23,24)\}$ has the property that $\sum 1/m_i = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/8 + 1/12 + 1/24 = 1$, exactly tiling $\mathbb{Z}$ — this covering property is machine-checked (`decide`), and the divisibility consequence is later assembled into a full, unconditional obstruction rather than left as an axiom.

title: Density Bounds
content: lowerDensity(ExceptionalSet) > 0 is now a PROVED theorem, not an axiom: `exceptionalCount_positive_density` and `lowerDensity_exceptionalSet_pos` (in the 'Erdős 1950, full strength' section below) establish it constructively, showing at least N/22369620 exceptional integers below every horizon N ≥ 2^52. The upper bound lowerDensity(ExceptionalSet) < 1/10 (~9% of all integers, ~18% of odd integers) remains documented only — not formalized.
mathContext: The positive lower-density half of the bound $0 < \underline{d}(E)$ is now machine-checked (Session 6), sharpening the earlier axiom-free infinitude result to an explicit quantitative density. The upper bound $\underline{d}(E) < 1/10$, which would show most odd integers are still Romanoff, is not formalized.

title: Foundational Lemmas (Axiom-Free)
content: The machine-checked core: `mem_exceptionalSet_iff` unfolds membership; `isRomanoff_four_le` gives the structural floor n ≥ 4 for Romanoff n; `not_isRomanoff_one`/`not_isRomanoff_three` place 1 and 3 in the exceptional set; `isRomanoff_five`/`isRomanoff_seven` give concrete witnesses; `density_nonneg`/`density_le_one` bound the density functional to [0,1]; `erdosCovering_isCoveringSystem` proves the {2,3,4,6,8,12,24} system genuinely covers ℤ, by `decide`; `isRomanoff_iff_mem_range` bounds the witness exponent to a finite range, giving a `Decidable (IsRomanoff n)` instance; and 127, 149, 251, 331 are verified exceptional by `decide` using that instance.
mathContext: Everything here depends only on $\text{propext}/\text{Classical.choice}/\text{Quot.sound}$. The key device, `isRomanoff_iff_mem_range`, bounds the witness exponent $k$ (since $2^k < n$ forces $k < 2^k < n$), making `IsRomanoff` decidable and the exceptionality of specific OEIS A006285 terms machine-checkable.

title: The Covering-Congruence Obstruction Mechanism (Axiom-Free)
content: The verified gear behind the covering construction: `two_pow_mod_three` (2^k mod 3 has period 2), `two_pow_modEq_of_dvd` (order-periodicity of 2 mod a prime p with 2^d ≡ 1 mod p), the general obstruction `covering_prime_not_prime_sub` (if p ∣ n − 2^k on the residue class where k ≡ r mod d, and n − 2^k > p, then n − 2^k is composite), and the concrete gears `not_prime_sub_even_mod_three` (prime 3 kills even exponents) and `not_prime_sub_mod_seven` (prime 7 kills exponents divisible by 3). All axiom-free.
mathContext: Fixing a prime $p$ with $\text{ord}_p(2) = d$, on the residue class $k \equiv r \pmod d$ the value $n - 2^k$ is divisible by $p$; if it also exceeds $p$ it cannot be prime. This is the mechanism, applied one prime/residue-class at a time, that eventually eliminates every exponent class and produces an arithmetic progression of exceptional $n$.

title: Assembling the Gears: The Full Covering Obstruction (Axiom-Free)
content: Runs the full covering system on the *exponent*: the six classes k ≡ 0 (2), 0 (3), 1 (4), 3 (8), 7 (12), 23 (24) cover ℤ, each closed by a prime whose order of 2 equals that modulus — 3, 7, 5, 17, 13, 241 (order gears proved by `decide`/`norm_num`). The assembled theorem `covering_obstruction_not_isRomanoff` shows any n meeting six explicit CRT residues plus a size hypothesis (n − 2^k > 241 for every valid k) is not Romanoff, and `covering_progression_mem_exceptionalSet` packages the odd such n as members of `ExceptionalSet` — the membership form of Erdős's 1950 theorem. All axiom-free.
mathContext: Six primes with $\text{ord}_p(2) = d$ close a covering system of the exponent $k$; by CRT, the progression $n \equiv a \pmod{3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\cdot17\cdot241}$ makes every $n - 2^k$ composite once it exceeds 241, so the whole progression (subject to that one size hypothesis) lies in `ExceptionalSet` — Erdős (1950), assembled unconditionally.

title: Erdős's Infinite Arithmetic Progression: The Exceptional Set is Infinite
content: Promotes the CRT membership form into an unconditional infinitude result. `exists_exceptional_gt`: for every bound B there is an exceptional n > B, obtained by picking a progression member large enough that the size hypothesis holds automatically. `exceptionalSet_infinite`: `ExceptionalSet.Infinite` follows immediately — the full Erdős (1950) theorem that infinitely many odd numbers are not of the form 2^k + p, proved axiom-free.
mathContext: From the covering progression modulo $3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\cdot17\cdot241$ one extracts, above any bound $B$, an odd $n$ with every $n-2^k$ composite; hence $\text{ExceptionalSet}$ is unbounded and therefore infinite, with no axioms.

title: Erdős (1950), Full Strength: The Exceptional Set Has Positive Lower Density
content: Strengthens infinitude to positive lower density, all axiom-free. `coveringAP`/`Trapped` feed `coveringAP_mem_exceptionalSet` (every untrapped progression member is exceptional); `card_trapped_le` bounds trapped members below a horizon N to at most log₂ N + 1 (each dyadic window traps at most one member, since it is far shorter than the common difference); `exceptionalCount_lower_bound`/`exceptionalCount_positive_density` combine these into at least N/11184810 − (log₂ N + 1) exceptional integers below N, exceeding N/22369620 once N ≥ 2^52; `density_exceptionalSet_ge`/`lowerDensity_exceptionalSet_pos` package this as `0 < lowerDensity ExceptionalSet`.
mathContext: The linear main term $N/11184810$ (one progression member per period) dwarfs the logarithmic trapped-member loss $\log_2 N + 1$ once $N$ is large, giving a genuine positive-density lower bound rather than mere infinitude — Erdős's 1950 result at full strength, proved unconditionally and axiom-free.
